import base64
import email.utils
import hashlib
import hmac
import socket
import subprocess
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import uuid
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

account = 'devstoreaccount1'
key = base64.b64decode('Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==')
name = 'phase1verify' + uuid.uuid4().hex
opener = urllib.request.build_opener(urllib.request.ProxyHandler({}))

def request(port, method, resource, body=b'', extra=None, expected=200):
    url = f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{account}/{resource}'
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlsplit(url)
    headers = {'x-ms-date': email.utils.formatdate(usegmt=True), 'x-ms-version': '2021-12-02'}
    headers.update(extra or {})
    canonical_headers = ''.join(f'{k}:{v}\n' for k, v in sorted(headers.items()) if k.startswith('x-ms-'))
    canonical_resource = '/' + account + parsed.path
    for k, values in sorted(urllib.parse.parse_qs(parsed.query).items()):
        canonical_resource += '\n' + k.lower() + ':' + ','.join(sorted(values))
    fields = [method, '', '', str(len(body)) if body else '', '', headers.get('Content-Type', ''), '', '', '', '', '', '']
    signature = base64.b64encode(hmac.new(key, ('\n'.join(fields) + '\n' + canonical_headers + canonical_resource).encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode()
    headers['Authorization'] = f'SharedKey {account}:{signature}'
    data = body if method in ('PUT', 'POST') else None
    with opener.open(urllib.request.Request(url, data=data, headers=headers, method=method), timeout=10) as response:
        assert response.status == expected, (method, resource, response.status)
        return response.read()

def mongo(script):
    subprocess.run(['podman', 'exec', 'product-support-agent-mongodb-1', 'mongosh', '--quiet', '--eval', script], check=True, timeout=20)

queue_created = False
blob_created = False
mongo_created = False
try:
    with socket.create_connection(('127.0.0.1', 27017), timeout=10):
        print('MongoDB host port reachable')
    mongo(f'const d = db.getSiblingDB("{name}"); d.probe.insertOne({{value:"synthetic-phase1"}}); if (d.probe.findOne().value !== "synthetic-phase1") throw new Error("MongoDB round trip failed"); print("MongoDB write/read passed");')
    mongo_created = True
    request(10001, 'PUT', name, expected=201)
    queue_created = True
    request(10001, 'POST', name + '/messages', b'<QueueMessage><MessageText>synthetic-phase1</MessageText></QueueMessage>', {'Content-Type':'application/xml'}, expected=201)
    request(10000, 'PUT', name + '?restype=container', expected=201)
    blob_created = True
    request(10000, 'PUT', name + '/probe.txt', b'synthetic-phase1', {'x-ms-blob-type':'BlockBlob','Content-Type':'text/plain'}, expected=201)
    assert request(10000, 'GET', name + '/probe.txt') == b'synthetic-phase1'
    assert ET.fromstring(request(10001, 'GET', name + '/messages?peekonly=true')).findtext('./QueueMessage/MessageText') == 'synthetic-phase1'
    print('Azurite host queue and blob authenticated write/read passed')
    subprocess.run(['podman', 'restart', 'product-support-agent-mongodb-1', 'product-support-agent-azurite-1'], check=True, timeout=60)
    time.sleep(5)
    mongo(f'const d = db.getSiblingDB("{name}"); if (d.probe.findOne().value !== "synthetic-phase1") throw new Error("MongoDB persistence failed"); print("MongoDB restart persistence passed");')
    assert request(10000, 'GET', name + '/probe.txt') == b'synthetic-phase1'
    message = ET.fromstring(request(10001, 'GET', name + '/messages')).find('QueueMessage')
    assert message is not None and message.findtext('MessageText') == 'synthetic-phase1'
    query = urllib.parse.urlencode({'popreceipt':message.findtext('PopReceipt')})
    request(10001, 'DELETE', name + '/messages/' + message.findtext('MessageId') + '?' + query, expected=204)
    assert ET.fromstring(request(10001, 'GET', name + '/messages?peekonly=true')).find('QueueMessage') is None
    print('Azurite restart persistence and queue message acknowledgement passed')
finally:
    if queue_created:
        request(10001, 'DELETE', name, expected=204)
    if blob_created:
        request(10000, 'DELETE', name + '?restype=container', expected=202)
    if mongo_created:
        mongo(f'db.getSiblingDB("{name}").dropDatabase(); print("Synthetic MongoDB data removed");')
    print('Synthetic verification data removed')

The following material is provided as clarification for the subject of shutting down socket connections closing the sockets. It is important to distinguish the difference between shutting down a socket connection and closing a socket.
Shutting down a socket connection involves an exchange of protocol messages between the two endpoints, hereafter referred to as a shutdown sequence. Two general classes of shutdown sequences are defined: graceful and abortive (also called hard). In a graceful shutdown sequence, any data that has been queued, but not yet transmitted can be sent prior to the connection being closed. In an abortive shutdown, any unsent data is lost. The occurrence of a shutdown sequence (graceful or abortive) can also be used to provide an FD\_CLOSE indication to the associated applications signifying that a shutdown is in progress.
Closing a socket, on the other hand, causes the socket handle to become deallocated so that the application can no longer reference or use the socket in any manner.
In Windows Sockets, both the [**shutdown**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-shutdown) function, and the [**WSASendDisconnect**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/Winsock2/nf-winsock2-wsasenddisconnect) function can be used to initiate a shutdown sequence, while the [**closesocket**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-closesocket) function is used to deallocate socket handles and free up any associated resources. Some amount of confusion arises, however, from the fact that the **closesocket** function implicitly causes a shutdown sequence to occur if it has not already happened. In fact, it has become a rather common programming practice to rely on this feature and to use **closesocket** to both initiate the shutdown sequence and deallocate the socket handle.
To facilitate this usage, the sockets interface provides for controls by way of the socket option mechanism that allow the programmer to indicate whether the implicit shutdown sequence should be graceful or abortive, and also whether the [**closesocket**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-closesocket) function should linger (that is not complete immediately) to allow time for a graceful shutdown sequence to complete. These important distinctions and the ramifications of using **closesocket** in this manner are still not widely understood.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/winsock/graceful-shutdown-linger-options-and-socket-closure-2"},{"title":"Manage state and data in Docker applications","content":"# Manage state and data in Docker applications
Tip
This content is an excerpt from the eBook, .NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications, available on [.NET Docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices) or as a free downloadable PDF that can be read offline.
![.NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications eBook cover thumbnail.](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/architecture/microservices/media/cover-thumbnail.png)
In most cases, you can think of a container as an instance of a process. A process doesn't maintain persistent state. While a container can write to its local storage, assuming that an instance will be around indefinitely would be like assuming that a single location in memory will be durable. You should assume that container images, like processes, have multiple instances or will eventually be killed. If they're managed with a container orchestrator, you should assume that they might get moved from one node or VM to another.
The following solutions are used to manage data in Docker applications:
From the Docker host, as [Docker Volumes](https://docs.docker.com/engine/admin/volumes/):
1. **Volumes** are stored in an area of the host filesystem that's managed by Docker.
2. **Bind mounts** can map to any folder in the host filesystem, so access can't be controlled from Docker process and can pose a security risk as a container could access sensitive OS folders.
3. **tmpfs mounts** are like virtual folders that only exist in the host's memory and are never written to the filesystem.
From remote storage:
1. [Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-introduction), which provides geo-distributable storage, providing a good long-term persistence solution for containers.
2. Remote relational databases like [Azure SQL Database](https://azure.microsoft.com/services/sql-database/) or NoSQL databases like [Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/introduction), or cache services like [Redis](https://redis.io/).

## Shutdown
The containers shut down in the following situations:
1. When a container app scales in
2. When a container app is deleted
3. When a revision is deactivated
When a shutdown starts, the container host sends a [SIGTERM message](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_%28IPC%29) to your container. The code in the container can respond to this operating system-level message to handle termination.
If your application doesn't respond within 30 seconds to the `SIGTERM` message, then [SIGKILL](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_%28IPC%29) terminates your container.
Make sure your application can gracefully handle shutdowns. Containers restart regularly, so don't expect state to persist inside a container. Instead, use external caches for expensive in-memory cache requirements.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/application-lifecycle-management#shutdown"},{"title":"Configure and customize SQL Server Linux containers (cs1-bash)","content":"# Configure and customize SQL Server Linux containers (cs1-bash)
## Persist your data
Your SQL Server configuration changes and database files are persisted in the container even if you restart the container with `docker stop` and `docker start`. However, if you remove the container with `docker rm`, everything in the container is deleted, including SQL Server and your databases. The following section explains how to use *data volumes* to persist your database files even if the associated containers are deleted.
Important
For SQL Server, it's critical that you understand data persistence in Docker. In addition to the discussion in this section, see Docker's documentation on [how to manage data in Docker containers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes).
### Mount a host directory as a data volume
The first option is to mount a directory on your host as a data volume in your container. To do that, use the `docker run` command with the `-v <host directory>:/var/opt/mssql` flag, where `<host directory>` is any given path. For instance: `C:\SQL` on Windows, or `~/sqlvolumes` on Linux. This allows the data to be restored between container executions.
Note
Containers for SQL Server 2019 (15.x) and later versions automatically start up as non-root, while SQL Server 2017 (14.x) containers start as root by default. For more information on running SQL Server containers as non-root, see [Secure SQL Server Linux containers](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/linux/containers/security?view=sql-server-ver17).
Important
The `SA_PASSWORD` environment variable is deprecated. Use `MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD` instead.
```bash
docker run -e 'ACCEPT_EULA=Y' -e 'MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD=<password>' \
-p 1433:1433 \
-v <host directory>/data:/var/opt/mssql/data \
-v <host directory>/log:/var/opt/mssql/log \
-v <host directory>/secrets:/var/opt/mssql/secrets \
-d mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest
```
Caution
Your password should follow the SQL Server default [password policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/security/password-policy?view=sql-server-ver17). By default, the password must be at least eight characters long and contain characters from three of the following four sets: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, base-10 digits, and symbols. Passwords can be up to 128 characters long. 1. **Overlay File System**. This Docker feature implements a copy-on-write task that stores updated information to the root file system of the container. That information is "on top" of the original image on which the container is based. If the container is deleted from the system, those changes are lost. Therefore, while it's possible to save the state of a container within its local storage, designing a system around this would conflict with the premise of container design, which by default is stateless.
However, using Docker Volumes is now the preferred way to handle local data in Docker. If you need more information about storage in containers check on [Docker storage drivers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/) and [About storage drivers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/).
The following provides more detail about these options:
**Volumes** are directories mapped from the host OS to directories in containers. When code in the container has access to the directory, that access is actually to a directory on the host OS. This directory is not tied to the lifetime of the container itself, and the directory is managed by Docker and isolated from the core functionality of the host machine. Thus, data volumes are designed to persist data independently of the life of the container. If you delete a container or an image from the Docker host, the data persisted in the data volume isn't deleted.
Volumes can be named or anonymous (the default). Named volumes are the evolution of **Data Volume Containers** and make it easy to share data between containers. Volumes also support volume drivers that allow you to store data on remote hosts, among other options.
**Bind mounts** are available since a long time ago and allow the mapping of any folder to a mount point in a container. Bind mounts have more limitations than volumes and some important security issues, so volumes are the recommended option.
**tmpfs mounts** are basically virtual folders that live only in the host's memory and are never written to the filesystem. They are fast and secure but use memory and are only meant for temporary, non-persistent data.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/architecture/microservices/architect-microservice-container-applications/docker-application-state-data"},{"title":"Graceful Shutdown, Linger Options, and Socket Closure","content":"# Graceful Shutdown, Linger Options, and Socket Closure
The following material is provided as clarification for the subject of shutting down socket connections closing the sockets. It is important to distinguish the difference between shutting down a socket connection and closing a socket.
Shutting down a socket connection involves an exchange of protocol messages between the two endpoints, hereafter referred to as a shutdown sequence. Two general classes of shutdown sequences are defined: graceful and abortive (also called hard). In a graceful shutdown sequence, any data that has been queued, but not yet transmitted can be sent prior to the connection being closed. In an abortive shutdown, any unsent data is lost. The occurrence of a shutdown sequence (graceful or abortive) can also be used to provide an FD\_CLOSE indication to the associated applications signifying that a shutdown is in progress.
Closing a socket, on the other hand, causes the socket handle to become deallocated so that the application can no longer reference or use the socket in any manner.
In Windows Sockets, both the [**shutdown**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-shutdown) function, and the [**WSASendDisconnect**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/Winsock2/nf-winsock2-wsasenddisconnect) function can be used to initiate a shutdown sequence, while the [**closesocket**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-closesocket) function is used to deallocate socket handles and free up any associated resources. Some amount of confusion arises, however, from the fact that the **closesocket** function implicitly causes a shutdown sequence to occur if it has not already happened. In fact, it has become a rather common programming practice to rely on this feature and to use **closesocket** to both initiate the shutdown sequence and deallocate the socket handle.
To facilitate this usage, the sockets interface provides for controls by way of the socket option mechanism that allow the programmer to indicate whether the implicit shutdown sequence should be graceful or abortive, and also whether the [**closesocket**](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/winsock/nf-winsock-closesocket) function should linger (that is not complete immediately) to allow time for a graceful shutdown sequence to complete. These important distinctions and the ramifications of using **closesocket** in this manner are still not widely understood.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/winsock/graceful-shutdown-linger-options-and-socket-closure-2"},{"title":"Manage state and data in Docker applications","content":"# Manage state and data in Docker applications

This content is an excerpt from the eBook, .NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications, available on [.NET Docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices) or as a free downloadable PDF that can be read offline.
![.NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications eBook cover thumbnail.](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/architecture/microservices/media/cover-thumbnail.png)
In most cases, you can think of a container as an instance of a process. A process doesn't maintain persistent state. While a container can write to its local storage, assuming that an instance will be around indefinitely would be like assuming that a single location in memory will be durable. You should assume that container images, like processes, have multiple instances or will eventually be killed. If they're managed with a container orchestrator, you should assume that they might get moved from one node or VM to another.
The following solutions are used to manage data in Docker applications:
From the Docker host, as [Docker Volumes](https://docs.docker.com/engine/admin/volumes/):
1. **Volumes** are stored in an area of the host filesystem that's managed by Docker.
2. **Bind mounts** can map to any folder in the host filesystem, so access can't be controlled from Docker process and can pose a security risk as a container could access sensitive OS folders.
3. **tmpfs mounts** are like virtual folders that only exist in the host's memory and are never written to the filesystem.
From remote storage:
1. [Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-introduction), which provides geo-distributable storage, providing a good long-term persistence solution for containers.
2. Remote relational databases like [Azure SQL Database](https://azure.microsoft.com/services/sql-database/) or NoSQL databases like [Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/introduction), or cache services like [Redis](https://redis.io/).

import base64, email.utils, hashlib, hmac, subprocess, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request, uuid
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
name='phase1verify'+uuid.uuid4().hex
account='devstoreaccount1'
key=base64.b64decode('Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==')
opener=urllib.request.build_opener(urllib.request.ProxyHandler({}))
def req(port,method,path,body=b'',extra=None,status=200):
    url=f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{account}/{path}'
    p=urllib.parse.urlsplit(url)
    h={'x-ms-date':email.utils.formatdate(usegmt=True),'x-ms-version':'2021-12-02','Content-Type':'application/octet-stream'}
    h.update(extra or {})
    ch=''.join(f'{k}:{v}\n' for k,v in sorted(h.items()) if k.startswith('x-ms-'))
    cr='/'+account+p.path+''.join('\n'+k+':'+','.join(sorted(v)) for k,v in sorted(urllib.parse.parse_qs(p.query).items()))
    fields=[method,'','',str(len(body)) if body else '','',h['Content-Type'],'','','','','','']
    sig=base64.b64encode(hmac.new(key,('\n'.join(fields)+'\n'+ch+cr).encode(),hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode()
    h['Authorization']=f'SharedKey {account}:{sig}'
    with opener.open(urllib.request.Request(url,data=body if method in ('PUT','POST') else None,headers=h,method=method),timeout=10) as r:
        assert r.status==status,(path,r.status)
        return r.read()
print('Synthetic resource:',name,flush=True)
req(10001,'PUT',name,status=201)
req(10001,'POST',name+'/messages',b'<QueueMessage><MessageText>synthetic-phase1</MessageText></QueueMessage>',{'Content-Type':'application/xml'},201)
req(10000,'PUT',name+'?restype=container',status=201)
req(10000,'PUT',name+'/probe',b'synthetic-phase1',{'x-ms-blob-type':'BlockBlob'},201)
subprocess.run(['podman','stop','--time','30','product-support-agent-azurite-1'],check=True,timeout=45)
subprocess.run(['podman','start','product-support-agent-azurite-1'],check=True,timeout=20)
time.sleep(5)
try:
    assert req(10000,'GET',name+'/probe')==b'synthetic-phase1'
    msg=ET.fromstring(req(10001,'GET',name+'/messages')).find('QueueMessage')
    assert msg is not None and msg.findtext('MessageText')=='synthetic-phase1'
    qs=urllib.parse.urlencode({'popreceipt':msg.findtext('PopReceipt')})
    req(10001,'DELETE',name+'/messages/'+msg.findtext('MessageId')+'?'+qs,status=204)
    assert ET.fromstring(req(10001,'GET',name+'/messages?peekonly=true')).find('QueueMessage') is None
    print('Azurite stop/start persistence and queue acknowledgement passed',flush=True)
finally:
    for port,path,status in [(10001,name,204),(10000,name+'?restype=container',202)]:
        try:
            req(port,'DELETE',path,status=status)
            print('Removed synthetic resource on port',port,flush=True)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if e.code!=404: raise
            print('Synthetic resource already absent on port',port,flush=True)
